power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of cortical sites connected with the hippocampus improves scores on episodic memory tests and is being tested for memory decline, including in Alzheimer's disease.
These gains are read as gains in intentional retrieval.
Objective: To examine whether standard memory outcomes can support this reading and how the contribution of repetition priming can be measured.

Methods: Narrative review of hippocampal-network stimulation studies, cognitive and electrophysiological research on priming and processing fluency, stimulation studies of priming and parietal cortex, and clinical trials of TMS for memory decline.
Results: Old/new recognition and cued recall present studied items or cues again at test.
Repetition priming makes these items easier to process, and this fluency can raise a memory score with intentional retrieval unchanged.
The fluency behind word-recognition decisions is largely conceptual, so it persists after a change of surface form.
TMS can also alter priming directly, and stimulating the standard parietal target changes the subjective side of recollection.

Meta-analytic evidence shows that the gains are specific to episodic memory and largest for recollection tests after stimulation before encoding, but the priming contribution to these gains has not been estimated.
Conclusions: Process-level claims about stimulation-related memory gains require the priming contribution to be measured.
Five measurement steps, centred on matched indirect tests and process-dissociation procedures, make it measurable in the same participants, including in clinical trials.

Episodic memory involves the conscious recollection of a specific past event, whereas implicit memory is expressed when prior experience influences performance without conscious or intentional recollection [1, 2].
text.formatted: Episodic memory involves the conscious recollection of a specific past event, whereas implicit memory is expressed when prior experience influences performance without conscious or intentional recollection <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: Here, this distinction is used to refer to how memory is expressed at test.
Priming refers to the facilitation of subsequent processing produced by prior exposure.
Processing fluency refers to the subjective ease of processing that may result from this facilitation.
Participants may interpret this ease as evidence that an item was encountered previously and use it to inform recognition judgements [3, 4].
text.formatted: Participants may interpret this ease as evidence that an item was encountered previously and use it to inform recognition judgements <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4]</ref>.

text.text: Recent syntheses describe the subjective feeling of familiarity as fluency attributed to past encounters, a fluency that can have mnemonic and non-mnemonic sources [5].
text.formatted: Recent syntheses describe the subjective feeling of familiarity as fluency attributed to past encounters, a fluency that can have mnemonic and non-mnemonic sources <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: In tasks that re-present studied material at test, performance may therefore reflect repetition priming and the processing fluency it can produce alongside episodic retrieval.
A single outcome measure may contain contributions from multiple memory processes [6, 7].
text.formatted: A single outcome measure may contain contributions from multiple memory processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: A direct assessment of these implicit influences requires an indirect priming measure matched to the explicit memory test.
Assessing explicit and indirect performance together makes their potential contributions more measurable and comparable within the same participants and materials.

This measurement problem is particularly consequential in transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) studies, in which improvements in task performance are interpreted as improvements in episodic-memory function.
TMS has been used for more than two decades to modulate episodic memory through stimulation of different cortical targets.
Following early interference studies of the prefrontal cortex [8, 9], the literature expanded substantially.
text.formatted: Following early interference studies of the prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>, the literature expanded substantially.

text.text: A systematic review included 59 TMS studies of episodic memory [10].
text.formatted: A systematic review included 59 TMS studies of episodic memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>.

text.text: One influential approach within this research programme is the network-based stimulation paradigm introduced in 2014 [11].
text.formatted: One influential approach within this research programme is the network-based stimulation paradigm introduced in 2014 <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>.

text.text: That study applied multi-session repetitive TMS (rTMS) to a left lateral parietal site chosen for its resting-state functional connectivity with the hippocampus.
It reported increased connectivity within the hippocampal network alongside improved face-cued word recall.
Because conventional TMS cannot directly reach the hippocampus, the approach stimulates an accessible cortical node to influence the hippocampal network indirectly.
This approach is now termed hippocampal indirectly targeted stimulation (HITS).
The paradigm was subsequently extended to older adults, individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease [12] [13] [14] [15], and psychiatric populations [16].
text.formatted: The paradigm was subsequently extended to older adults, individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer's disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, and psychiatric populations <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: Subsequent studies from the original laboratory and from independent groups have largely reproduced the memory effect [17] [18] [19] [20] [21] [22].
text.formatted: Subsequent studies from the original laboratory and from independent groups have largely reproduced the memory effect <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref>.

text.text: A re-analysis of an independent multi-day study that had found no memory effect showed larger memory gains in participants whose stimulation site lay closer to an individually personalised target [23].
text.formatted: A re-analysis of an independent multi-day study that had found no memory effect showed larger memory gains in participants whose stimulation site lay closer to an individually personalised target <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">[23]</ref>.

text.text: The programme has since moved into longer clinical trials, including a 52-week randomised trial of precuneus rTMS in Alzheimer's disease [24].
text.formatted: The programme has since moved into longer clinical trials, including a 52-week randomised trial of precuneus rTMS in Alzheimer's disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: A quantitative synthesis of 38 HITS studies reported a small-to-moderate improvement in episodic memory (Hedges' g = 0.44) [25].
text.formatted: A quantitative synthesis of 38 HITS studies reported a small-to-moderate improvement in episodic memory (Hedges' g = 0.44) <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: The effect on non-memory tasks was close to zero (g = 0.04).
The effect was larger for tasks emphasising recollection than for recognition tasks, a pattern interpreted as evidence of cognitive and mechanistic specificity.
The effect was also larger when stimulation preceded encoding, and it was largest when stimulation before encoding was combined with a recollection test (g = 0.66), the design of the original study.
Stimulation after encoding produced an average effect close to zero.
The advantage for recollection tests argues against a simple item-fluency account, under which old/new recognition, the format most open to fluency, would show the largest gains.
These findings support specificity across task domains.
Establishing specificity at the process level additionally requires the separate measurement of episodic retrieval and priming contributions.
Stimulation before encoding can shape both explicit and implicit traces, and cued recall still re-presents a studied cue, so neither moderator identifies the process by itself.
Here we set out the test formats through which priming can contribute to these scores.
We also review evidence that stimulation reaches priming and alters recollective experience at the parietal target.
The following sections then address why this contribution stays unmeasured and what it means in patient groups and clinical trials.
They close with five measurement steps that separate priming from retrieval in the same participants.
Behavioural tasks separate explicit and implicit memory processes only in part.
Performance on direct tests can be influenced by automatic processes, whereas performance on indirect tests can be affected by intentional retrieval and strategic responding.
Both direct and indirect memory tasks are therefore process-impure [26].
text.formatted: Both direct and indirect memory tasks are therefore process-impure <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Impure measures can still be separated.
A single explicit score leaves the contributions confounded, with no means of estimating either.
A matched indirect measure or a process-dissociation procedure turns the assumption that the score reflects retrieval alone into an empirical comparison within the same participants and materials.
Masked primes flashed just before a recognition decision change both "old" responses and the brain potential linked to familiarity.
Relative to primes that match the test word, orthographically similar primes produce fewer "old" responses and more negative potentials 300 to 500 ms after the word [27].
text.formatted: Relative to primes that match the test word, orthographically similar primes produce fewer "old" responses and more negative potentials 300 to 500 ms after the word <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Reducing perceptual overlap while holding meaning constant leaves the effect intact, whereas removing conceptual overlap abolishes it, so the fluency driving these decisions is largely conceptual [28].
text.formatted: Reducing perceptual overlap while holding meaning constant leaves the effect intact, whereas removing conceptual overlap abolishes it, so the fluency driving these decisions is largely conceptual <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">[28]</ref>.

text.text: In a recognition test, repeated words produced a frontal old/new effect linked to familiarity [29].
text.formatted: In a recognition test, repeated words produced a frontal old/new effect linked to familiarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: When repeated words were judged for pleasantness, the old/new effect resembled an N400 effect.

Recognition can also be accurate without reported awareness of retrieval, both behaviourally and in its electrophysiological signature [30, 31], although an attempt to reproduce the behavioural effect in three experiments was unsuccessful [32].
text.formatted: Recognition can also be accurate without reported awareness of retrieval, both behaviourally and in its electrophysiological signature <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">31]</ref>, although an attempt to reproduce the behavioural effect in three experiments was unsuccessful <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: Together, these studies show that processing fluency can contribute to some recognition judgements and that the same behavioural outcome can be produced by more than one process.
A single-system account reads these effects differently.
In patients with amnesia, a formal model with one memory signal predicted the pattern of recognition and repetition priming for the same objects, including deficits in both [33].
text.formatted: In patients with amnesia, a formal model with one memory signal predicted the pattern of recognition and repetition priming for the same objects, including deficits in both <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: On that account, priming and recognition are two readouts of one signal.
The measurement argument holds under both accounts.
In each case a recognition score combines contributions that a matched indirect measure can estimate separately.
The opportunity created by re-presentation can be seen in one of the central tasks of this research programme.
In the face-word task of the original HITS study, participants studied words paired with faces and later attempted to recall the associated word when the same face was presented again at test.
Easier processing of a previously encountered face differs from remembering its associated word, and by itself it cannot produce the correct response.
Fluency in processing the cue could still contribute to the explicit response through attention, decisionmaking or access to associated information.
This mechanism is inferred by applying the priming literature reviewed above to the structure of the task.
The original study included no measure of it.
A matched indirect measure would allow this cue fluency to be assessed alongside intentional episodic retrieval.
Tasks that re-present studied material differ in how open they are to this contribution (Fig. 1).
text.formatted: Tasks that re-present studied material differ in how open they are to this contribution (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: In recognition tests that require old and new items to be distinguished, the relatively fluent processing of a studied item can directly support an "old" response.
The contribution is less direct when a studied cue is re-presented to elicit an associated response.
Cue fluency leaves the correct target unspecified, yet it may influence the process through which the response is produced.
In forced-choice or temporal-order tasks in which all response options were previously studied, the options share a similar repetition history.
Simple item fluency is then less diagnostic of the correct response.
Even in these tasks, repetition can affect the processing of re-presented materials, item-response bindings or decision processes [34].
text.formatted: Even in these tasks, repetition can affect the processing of re-presented materials, item-response bindings or decision processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref>.

text.text: The scoring of a test also matters.
Sensitivity measures such as d′ correct for a shift in response criterion.
Item-specific fluency raises hits on studied items without raising false alarms to new foils, so it raises d′ as well.
The lure-discrimination index of the Mnemonic Similarity Task, used in a HITS study of fear discrimination, works in the opposite direction [35].
text.formatted: The lure-discrimination index of the Mnemonic Similarity Task, used in a HITS study of fear discrimination, works in the opposite direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[35]</ref>.

text.text: A lure that feels fluent is more likely to be called old, so fluency lowers this index.
One study illustrates the importance of these distinctions [36].
text.formatted: One study illustrates the importance of these distinctions <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref>.

text.text: Although studied objects were re-presented at test, stimulation increased the precision of memory independently of overall retrieval success.
This pattern points to a more specific change than a simple item-fluency account would predict.
The possible contribution of priming should therefore be evaluated against the presence of re-presentation, the structure of the task and the nature of the behavioural outcome.
Stimulation can act on priming directly.
Magnetic stimulation of the right visual cortex impairs form-specific object priming [37].
text.formatted: Magnetic stimulation of the right visual cortex impairs form-specific object priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[37]</ref>.

text.text: An interventional study dissociated priming-based from working-memory-based attentional guidance in early visual cortex [38].
text.formatted: An interventional study dissociated priming-based from working-memory-based attentional guidance in early visual cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">[38]</ref>.

text.text: Both studies used outcomes outside episodic memory.
Together they show that priming is causally accessible to stimulation.
The parietal target also shapes how recollection is experienced.
Continuous theta-burst stimulation was applied to the left angular gyrus, part of the lateral parietal region that HITS studies target.
It kept the accuracy of source recollection high but selectively reduced confidence in it [39].
text.formatted: It kept the accuracy of source recollection high but selectively reduced confidence in it <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[39]</ref>.

text.text: The authors attribute this pattern to the integration of memory features into conscious experience.
The same stimulation reduced the retrieval of context features across sensory modalities and left the integration of features within one modality intact [40].
text.formatted: The same stimulation reduced the retrieval of context features across sensory modalities and left the integration of features within one modality intact <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">[40]</ref>.

text.text: Online stimulation of the left angular gyrus during encoding left recollection and familiarity estimates unchanged and altered confidence in incorrect judgements [41].
text.formatted: Online stimulation of the left angular gyrus during encoding left recollection and familiarity estimates unchanged and altered confidence in incorrect judgements <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">[41]</ref>.

text.text: An attentional account places the bottom-up capture of attention by retrieved information in ventral parietal cortex, which includes the angular gyrus [42].
text.formatted: An attentional account places the bottom-up capture of attention by retrieved information in ventral parietal cortex, which includes the angular gyrus <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">[42]</ref>.

text.text: A memory gain after parietal stimulation can therefore reflect a change in how memory signals are experienced and used, with or without a change in hippocampal retrieval.
Some studies have used control tasks from other cognitive domains to test the specificity of a TMS effect for episodic memory.
One study administered a probabilistic-classification task alongside a face-word task [43].
text.formatted: One study administered a probabilistic-classification task alongside a face-word task <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">[43]</ref>.

text.text: This comparison tests for a general improvement across different tasks.
The classification task uses different materials and test demands from the faceword task.
It therefore informs selectivity across cognitive domains and leaves the facilitation from repeated faces and words within the memory task unmeasured.
Changes in connectivity within the targeted network address a different but complementary question.

In the original study, its multi-day follow-up and the classification study, connectivity changes in the hippocampal network accompanied the memory gains, which shows that stimulation affected the intended neural system.
Identifying the psychological processes expressed in the behavioural score additionally requires direct and indirect behavioural measures to be considered together.
The neural target of an intervention and the cognitive processes through which that intervention is expressed in behaviour can thus be evaluated as related but distinct levels of evidence.
The outcome measures of this programme were designed to index hippocampal-dependent associative memory.
They score the accuracy of explicit responses.
Process-level claims are then drawn by comparing task formats, such as recollection-based with recognition-based tests.
Both formats are direct tests, so the comparison leaves the priming contribution to each format unestimated.
Priming enters the interpretation of stimulation studies as an explanation offered after the results.
Reductions in evoked activity after stimulation have been read as efficient processing, by analogy with findings from priming experiments [44], as in the precision study discussed above.
text.formatted: Reductions in evoked activity after stimulation have been read as efficient processing, by analogy with findings from priming experiments <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">[44]</ref>, as in the precision study discussed above.

text.text: Higher false-alarm rates after cerebellar stimulation have been read as stronger activation of associative links in semantic memory, in line with stimulation effects on associative priming [45].
text.formatted: Higher false-alarm rates after cerebellar stimulation have been read as stronger activation of associative links in semantic memory, in line with stimulation effects on associative priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">[45]</ref>.

text.text: A study of semantic prediction in reading considered an associativepriming account and set it aside [46].
text.formatted: A study of semantic prediction in reading considered an associativepriming account and set it aside <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">[46]</ref>.

text.text: Another report proposed that implicit memory guided responses in an explicit recognition test, drawing on the electrophysiological evidence reviewed above [47].
text.formatted: Another report proposed that implicit memory guided responses in an explicit recognition test, drawing on the electrophysiological evidence reviewed above <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">[47]</ref>.

text.text: An earlier study by our group read a gain in visual recognition after parietal rTMS in Alzheimer's disease as an improvement of implicit memory [48].
text.formatted: An earlier study by our group read a gain in visual recognition after parietal rTMS in Alzheimer's disease as an improvement of implicit memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">[48]</ref>.

text.text: Each of these interpretations uses explicit scores alone.
One study measured the contribution directly [49].
text.formatted: One study measured the contribution directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">[49]</ref>.

text.text: It administered indirect word-completion and explicit recognition measures to the same participants and excluded the words used in the completion test from the recognition analysis.
Disruption of the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex reduced the directed-forgetting effect on explicit recognition and left the effect on the indirect test unchanged.
The design shows that explicit and indirect effects of stimulation can be compared within one experiment.
The field can therefore show that stimulation changes memory scores and network connectivity, and that the change is selective across task domains.
It cannot yet show which memory process produced a given gain.
This distinction is particularly important in clinical samples.
Priming cannot be reduced to a single brain region or memory system.
The coordinate-based meta-analysis cited above covered 65 functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies.
Repetition suppression accompanying behavioural priming was concentrated in the left inferior frontal and fusiform gyri, and perceptual and conceptual priming showed no simple anatomical separation.
A clinical disorder or a particular TMS target therefore cannot be assumed to affect episodic memory, priming and their supporting networks to the same extent.
The role of the hippocampus remains contested.
A 2024 discussion paper reviewed 13 fMRI studies and found a confound, such as explicit memory or unbalanced attention, behind every reported hippocampal effect in implicit memory [50].
text.formatted: A 2024 discussion paper reviewed 13 fMRI studies and found a confound, such as explicit memory or unbalanced attention, behind every reported hippocampal effect in implicit memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">[50]</ref>.

text.text: Five commentaries disputed that conclusion, with arguments that included statistical learning, contextual cueing and findings with objectively invisible stimuli [51] [52] [53] [54] [55].
text.formatted: Five commentaries disputed that conclusion, with arguments that included statistical learning, contextual cueing and findings with objectively invisible stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">[51]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">[52]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">[53]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">[54]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">[55]</ref>.

text.text: One commentary supported it, noting that 7 of 18 studies linking the hippocampus with implicit memory reported no correction for multiple comparisons [56].
text.formatted: One commentary supported it, noting that 7 of 18 studies linking the hippocampus with implicit memory reported no correction for multiple comparisons <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">[56]</ref>.

text.text: The authors maintained their conclusion and called for conceptual clarity and more measures of awareness [57].
text.formatted: The authors maintained their conclusion and called for conceptual clarity and more measures of awareness <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">[57]</ref>.

text.text: If the hippocampus supports implicit memory, stimulation of the hippocampal network becomes more likely to act on priming; if the critique holds, it becomes less likely.
Current designs cannot test either possibility behaviourally.
Alzheimer's disease and amnestic mild cognitive impairment provide a clear example.
Recognition can be impaired from the earliest stages of Alzheimer's disease, including mild cognitive impairment [58].
text.formatted: Recognition can be impaired from the earliest stages of Alzheimer's disease, including mild cognitive impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">[58]</ref>.

text.text: In early Alzheimer's disease, impaired recognition of scenes has been reported alongside intact repetition priming for the same scenes, with different neural correlates for the two [59].
text.formatted: In early Alzheimer's disease, impaired recognition of scenes has been reported alongside intact repetition priming for the same scenes, with different neural correlates for the two <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">[59]</ref>.

text.text: Alzheimer pathology has also been associated with some measures of conceptual priming, without the same relationship for certain perceptual or word-completion measures [60].
text.formatted: Alzheimer pathology has also been associated with some measures of conceptual priming, without the same relationship for certain perceptual or word-completion measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">[60]</ref>.

text.text: A meta-analysis of 32 studies found repetition priming lower, on average, in both amnestic mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's dementia than in healthy older adults [61].
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of 32 studies found repetition priming lower, on average, in both amnestic mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's dementia than in healthy older adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">[61]</ref>.

text.text: The size of the difference varied across tasks and paradigms.

Where priming is relatively better preserved than episodic memory for a particular task, a re-presentation-based score may carry a larger share of priming than the level of intentional retrieval would suggest.
Related dissociations have been reported in other clinical groups.

In Parkinson's disease, free recall can be impaired in patients without dementia, and recall and recognition in patients with dementia, while word-and picture-fragment identification priming shows no impairment in either group [62].
text.formatted: In Parkinson's disease, free recall can be impaired in patients without dementia, and recall and recognition in patients with dementia, while word-and picture-fragment identification priming shows no impairment in either group <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">[62]</ref>.

text.text: Large-scale connectivity changes have also been described across the continuum of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease [63].
text.formatted: Large-scale connectivity changes have also been described across the continuum of cognitive impairment in Parkinson's disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">[63]</ref>.

text.text: Meta-analytic findings in schizophrenia indicate a small average impairment in priming, with reduced conceptual priming and intact perceptual priming [64].
text.formatted: Meta-analytic findings in schizophrenia indicate a small average impairment in priming, with reduced conceptual priming and intact perceptual priming <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">[64]</ref>.

text.text: Altered cortico-hippocampal network connectivity has also been associated with cognitive performance in first-episode schizophrenia [65].
text.formatted: Altered cortico-hippocampal network connectivity has also been associated with cognitive performance in first-episode schizophrenia <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">[65]</ref>.

text.text: Post-stroke cognitive impairment is accompanied by connectivity changes involving the hippocampus, precuneus and cingulate regions [66].
text.formatted: Post-stroke cognitive impairment is accompanied by connectivity changes involving the hippocampus, precuneus and cingulate regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">[66]</ref>.

text.text: Patients with occipital stroke have shown preserved conceptual category-exemplar priming alongside impaired perceptual picture-identification performance [67].
text.formatted: Patients with occipital stroke have shown preserved conceptual category-exemplar priming alongside impaired perceptual picture-identification performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">[67]</ref>.

text.text: Priming therefore varies across clinical populations, and its contribution should be evaluated within the relevant sample, materials and task format.
These dissociations bear directly on how stimulation trials are read.
Recent randomised trials in Alzheimer's disease, including the 52-week precuneus trial described above, use composite scales as primary and secondary endpoints.
These are the cognitive subscale of the Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale (ADAS-Cog), the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Clinical Dementia Rating Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB).
Of these, the word-recognition items of the ADAS-Cog present studied words again at test [68].
text.formatted: Of these, the word-recognition items of the ADAS-Cog present studied words again at test <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref>.

text.text: Effects on these scales are small and can be transient.
In an H-coil trial, real rTMS produced a mean decrease of 1.01 ADAS-Cog points per time point, a trend that was no longer evident two months after the end of treatment [69].
text.formatted: In an H-coil trial, real rTMS produced a mean decrease of 1.01 ADAS-Cog points per time point, a trend that was no longer evident two months after the end of treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref>.

text.text: In a multi-site trial, active and sham coils both produced significant cognitive improvement up to two months after treatment [70].
text.formatted: In a multi-site trial, active and sham coils both produced significant cognitive improvement up to two months after treatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref>.

text.text: Recently derived minimal clinically important differences for these scales exceed the average effects reported in recent trials of antiamyloid antibodies [71].
text.formatted: Recently derived minimal clinically important differences for these scales exceed the average effects reported in recent trials of antiamyloid antibodies <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[71]</ref>.

text.text: When an effect is this close to the threshold of clinical meaning, the process behind it decides what a trial has shown.
A gain in intentional retrieval would be expected to transfer to the everyday episodic function that the trials aim at.
A gain in facilitated processing of re-presented material would act on a process that one word-stem completion study found to match healthy older adults in Alzheimer's disease [72].
text.formatted: A gain in facilitated processing of re-presented material would act on a process that one word-stem completion study found to match healthy older adults in Alzheimer's disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[72]</ref>.

text.text: Such a gain has value as a different claim with a different therapeutic pathway.
Its benefit also needs evidence of its own.

Errorless learning, a rehabilitation technique thought to work through implicit memory, benefited young adults and gave older adults no advantage, and the effects of errorful learning related to explicit memory function [73].
text.formatted: Errorless learning, a rehabilitation technique thought to work through implicit memory, benefited young adults and gave older adults no advantage, and the effects of errorful learning related to explicit memory function <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[73]</ref>.

text.text: Measuring both contributions allows a trial to say which of these it has produced.
No single ideal task removes this problem.
Five steps make the possible contribution of priming visible and interpretable (Table 1). shape reproduction in the study of psychiatric patients described above.
text.formatted: Five steps make the possible contribution of priming visible and interpretable (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>). shape reproduction in the study of psychiatric patients described above.

text.text: Story recall [74] and complex-figure recall [75] serve the same purpose.
text.formatted: Story recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[74]</ref> and complex-figure recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">[75]</ref> serve the same purpose.

text.text: These formats reduce the direct contribution of repetition fluency because no studied item or cue is presented again at test.
When instruments such as the Auditory Verbal Learning Test are used, the recommendation applies to their freeand delayed-recall outcomes, since a recognition component re-presents studied material.
These tasks are also process-impure, yet they reduce the ambiguity that arises directly from item repetition at test.
Third, studies can combine outcomes with and without re-presentation in the same participants.
Reporting recognition alongside free-or delayed-recall measures tests if an effect generalises across test formats.
Our earlier study described above shows the value of joint reporting.
Its battery included immediate and delayed visual reproduction recall, visual recognition and verbal-memory measures, and the significant memory change appeared in visual recognition.
In clinical samples, an instrument whose structure contrasts free recall, cued recall and recognition is particularly informative.
Under the controlled encoding of the Free and Cued Selective Reminding Test, recall that cueing normalises indicates a retrieval deficit.
Recall that stays impaired despite cueing and recognition indicates a storage deficit, the amnestic profile of the medial temporal type [76, 77].
text.formatted: Recall that stays impaired despite cueing and recognition indicates a storage deficit, the amnestic profile of the medial temporal type <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77]</ref>.

text.text: Reporting these outcomes separately distinguishes an intervention that improves access to a stored representation from one that changes what is stored.
A single composite score cannot support that distinction.
Task scores can also have low reliability, and difference scores, such as change from baseline, depend on the reliability of their components and on the correlation between them [78].
text.formatted: Task scores can also have low reliability, and difference scores, such as change from baseline, depend on the reliability of their components and on the correlation between them <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref>.

text.text: The measures should preferably be administered at the same time points, and comparisons between them should be prespecified.
Fourth, studies can add a matched indirect test using the same materials.
The clearest design administers an indirect priming measure alongside the explicit-memory test, in the same participants and from the same pool of studied materials.
The matched design described above shows how non-overlapping item sets can be assigned to the two analyses.
Where possible, items should be counterbalanced across test formats, test order should be arranged to minimise contamination between tests, and no item should contribute to both analyses.
Fifth, studies can apply the process-dissociation procedure, which estimates controlled and automatic contributions within the same task structure [79].
text.formatted: Fifth, studies can apply the process-dissociation procedure, which estimates controlled and automatic contributions within the same task structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref>.

text.text: In the inclusion condition, participants complete a word stem with a word they remember from the study list, or with the first suitable word that comes to mind.
Both intentional retrieval and automatic priming can therefore produce a studied response.
In the exclusion condition, participants avoid words from the study list.
A studied word produced despite this instruction indicates an automatic influence.
Modelling inclusion and exclusion rates gives separate estimates of the two contributions (Box 1).
Both tools improve comparability without delivering process purity.
Process-dissociation estimates depend on assumptions about the relationship between processes and on comprehension of and compliance with the instructions.
Violations of the invariance assumption can bias the estimates and mislead their interpretation [80].
text.formatted: Violations of the invariance assumption can bias the estimates and mislead their interpretation <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[80]</ref>.

text.text: Studies should therefore report inclusion and exclusion rates alongside the estimates and check if the two estimates covary.
Indirect priming tests have already been run in amnestic mild cognitive impairment and Alzheimer's disease, as the patient studies discussed above show.
The literature reviewed here is heterogeneous in stimulation protocols, cortical targets, tasks, outcome measures and clinical populations.
Priming need not contribute to the same extent across studies, and its relationship with intentional retrieval has to be evaluated within each task and sample.

The same template applies to other neuromodulation programmes with cognitive outcomes: name the process that the endpoint leaves unmeasured, add a matched measure of it, and estimate both in the same participants.
Applied to memory, these steps would let the field state which process a stimulation-related gain reflects and which therapeutic pathway that gain opens.

Columns show what participants see at study, what they see or do at test and the fluency contribution that each format allows.

Drawings represent studied and new items, and icons and colours mark the four levels of contribution. a Old/new recognition: studied items reappear among new foils, so item fluency can directly support an "old" response. b Cued recall: the studied cue is re-presented and the associate must be produced, so cue fluency can act on the response process without supplying the target. c Stage-dependent or composite outcomes: in the example, an old/new item test precedes a source choice among options that were all studied.

Re-presentation at some stages only, or a repetition history shared by all response options, reduces the diagnostic value of item fluency. d Studied material absent at test: free recall, reproduction from memory and event reconstruction allow no direct item-fluency contribution.
The panels show where a contribution is possible; its mechanism and size require measurement.

What matched indirect tests and the process-dissociation procedure estimate A matched indirect test estimates priming as the difference between studied and unstudied items in an implicit task, such as stem completion, with items drawn from the same pool as the explicit test.

Comparing the stimulation effect on this difference with the effect on the explicit score shows which process changed.The process-dissociation procedure estimates controlled and automatic contributions from one task.

In the inclusion condition, a studied response can come from recollection (R) or, when recollection fails, from an automatic influence (A), so that inclusion = R + (1 -R)A. In the exclusion condition, a studied response appears only when recollection fails and the automatic influence acts, so that exclusion = (1 -R)A. Hence R = inclusion -exclusion and A = exclusion / (1 -R).
Both estimates assume that the two processes are independent and that the automatic influence is equal across conditions.
Reporting the raw rates lets readers check these assumptions.
